title: Random Tensors & Seeding 🎲
description: Create reproducible random numbers for initializations and shuffling.

slides.title: Why Randomness? 🎰
slides.content:
# Neural Nets Need Randomness
- Weight initialization
- Dropout layers
- Data shuffling

But for **reproducibility**, we control randomness with seeds.

TensorFlow provides `tf.random` module.

slides.title: Basic Random Functions
slides.content: Generate random values from different distributions.
slides.codeSnippet:
import tensorflow as tf

# Uniform [0,1) of shape (2,2)
unif = tf.random.uniform((2,2))
print(unif)

# Normal (mean=0, std=1)
norm = tf.random.normal((2,2))
print(norm)

# Integer uniform [0,10) shape (3,)
ints = tf.random.uniform((3,), maxval=10, dtype=tf.int32)
print(ints)

quizData.question: What range of values does `tf.random.uniform((4,), minval=2, maxval=5)` produce?

slides.title: Seeding for Reproducibility 🌱
slides.content:
# `tf.random.set_seed(seed)`

Sets the global seed. Run it once at the start.

```python
tf.random.set_seed(42)
a = tf.random.normal((2,))
tf.random.set_seed(42)
b = tf.random.normal((2,))  # a == b
```

For independent streams, use a `tf.random.Generator`.

slides.title: Using a Generator (Better)
slides.codeSnippet:
rng = tf.random.Generator.from_seed(1234)
a = rng.normal((3,))
b = rng.normal((3,))  # different, but reproducible if you re-create rng with same seed

quizData.question: If you set `tf.random.set_seed(42)` and then call `tf.random.normal((3,))` twice, you get the same values both times.
quizData.explanation: After setting the seed, the first call yields random numbers, the second call yields a different set because the RNG state advances.

slides.title: Shuffling Data 🔀
slides.content: Use `tf.random.shuffle(tensor)` to randomly permute along the first axis. This is crucial for training.
